name: Construction Worker
baseMeaning: A picture of a figure in an orange hard hat and yellow safety vest, smiling. Read in a message it lands as announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress.
tldr: 👷 Construction Worker. In a chat it comes across as announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress.

contextMeanings.meaning: The plain reading: a figure in an orange hard hat and yellow safety vest, smiling. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: Announcing a renovation you just started 👷

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress.
contextMeanings.example: Thanking the crew that fixed the leak 👷

contextMeanings.meaning: In a dating thread the gesture is usually doing the work of a line that was not typed. It arrives as announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress, softened by whatever sentence sits next to it.

In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.

platformNotes.note: In Slack 👷 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for announcing a renovation you just started, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.
On Discord 👷 is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.

On X and Twitter 👷 does most of its work in replies, where it tags a message like thanking the crew that fixed the leak. Short enough to survive being the whole post, which is exactly why it is used that way.

On iOS the Construction Worker 👷 renders as the neutral drawing, and the neutral swatch is what most people send without thinking about it. A message like announcing a renovation you just started is the kind that carries it — the picture lands before the sentence does.

WhatsApp renders 👷 exactly as the phone system does, but the keyboard keeps it in the person-role section, where nobody looks unless they are hunting for it. In family threads it tends to accompany a message like thanking the crew that fixed the leak.

generationalNotes.note: Gen Z reaches for 👷 to do the work of announcing a renovation you just started, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress.

Millennials tend to send 👷 deliberately, usually for something like thanking the crew that fixed the leak, and they read announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses 👷 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress into it than younger senders are.
Older senders use 👷 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress subtext in it.

warnings.description: The Mechanic 🧑‍🔧 is one tap away in every picker, and it does not carry the same reading — the mechanic reads as repair and troubleshooting, the construction worker reads as building and the site. Check which one you actually picked.

warnings.title: The reading it usually gets is not the one it was sent with

seoTitle: 👷 Construction Worker Emoji - What It Actually Means in Text
seoDescription: 👷 Construction Worker meaning: announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress. How the emoji is used at work, at home and in dating threads, and where it goes wrong.

longForm.overview:
The drawing of 👷 is a figure in an orange hard hat and yellow safety vest, smiling. It arrived with Unicode 6.0 in the person-role section, and in a conversation it does the work of a line somebody left out on purpose.

The line it stands in for is announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress. That is the reading most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one — a picture carries the same meaning as the sentence it replaces, and it arrives first.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets mistaken for a property-dispute warning when it is usually pride in doing the work — the vest signals builder, not menace. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 🧑‍🔧 Mechanic: the mechanic reads as repair and troubleshooting, the construction worker reads as building and the site. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

The construction worker also exists in five skin tones. They are separate pages with separate copy, because picking a tone is a decision in a way that picking the plain emoji is not: it says something about who the sender thinks the reader is.

In short — the construction worker reads as announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress, it is most often used for announcing a renovation you just started or thanking the crew that fixed the leak, and the five tone pages under it each say something different about who is sending it. The rest of the page takes those three apart.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
Context, not the picture, decides how this lands. 👷 in a work thread is thanking the crew that fixed the leak; 👷 in a family thread is announcing a renovation you just started; 👷 in a thread with somebody you like is a way of saying something you would rather not type out.

The tone versions of the emoji make the same point from the other side. The gesture is identical in all five, and the swatch says something about the sender before a word is read.

The shortest messages are the risky ones. A lone 👷 is the whole reply, and it is carrying a meaning nobody wrote down — announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress is the intention, but what arrives is a drawing. Everything the sentence would have disambiguated is simply missing.

Put it this way. Announcing a renovation you just started is the job the construction worker does most: it saves a sentence and lands faster than one would have. Thanking the crew that fixed the leak is the job it does second: there the picture is not the point, it is the temperature of the message.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Think about what the emoji is replacing. If the sentence under it is doing the real work, 👷 will get mistaken for a property-dispute warning when it is usually pride in doing the work — the vest signals builder, not menace instead, and the thread ends up carrying a meaning nobody wrote.

And keep it away from first contact. There is nothing warm in the drawing, and a construction worker gesture used to answer other people's messages tends to sound like it is settling a point.

Keep it out of the formal register. In a thread about somebody's work, or in a message to somebody you have not met, 👷 reads as announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress, and formality is exactly where that reading does the most damage.

Leave 🧑‍🔧 Mechanic for the other message. The mechanic reads as repair and troubleshooting, the construction worker reads as building and the site. And keep 👷 out of threads where somebody is hurting: it reads as announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress there, because there is nothing in the drawing that says you meant well.
longForm.howToReply:
The safe move in an unclear thread is to answer the text. 👷 gets mistaken for a property-dispute warning when it is usually pride in doing the work — the vest signals builder, not menace often enough that the sentence matters more than the picture.

And do not send 👷 alone when the message underneath is supposed to be warm. A message like announcing a renovation you just started carries the feeling; the picture on its own leaves the reader choosing between announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress and something sharper.

Start by reading what the 👷 was doing. If it was a reaction, react: 👷 back, and the thread is closed. If it was aimed at you, write. The difference matters, because the reply to a reaction can be a picture and the reply to a request cannot.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 👷 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under construction worker show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does 👷 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 👷 is used for announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress. The drawing shows a figure in an orange hard hat and yellow safety vest, smiling, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 👷 and 🧑‍🔧?
faqs.answer: The mechanic reads as repair and troubleshooting, the construction worker reads as building and the site. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is 👷 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress, but it gets mistaken for a property-dispute warning when it is usually pride in doing the work — the vest signals builder, not menace. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

faqs.question: What does 👷 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

conversationExamples.interpretation: A public sign-off, with the emoji as the full stop. The picture is doing the punctuation, which is why it is sent instead of a sentence.

conversationExamples.message: announcing a renovation you just started 👷
conversationExamples.interpretation: The everyday use: the picture carries the whole line. It lands as announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress, and matching it with the same emoji is a normal reply.

conversationExamples.message: thanking the crew that fixed the leak 👷
conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.

conversationExamples.message: there is something you should know 👷
conversationExamples.interpretation: A small joke or a nudge, with the emoji doing the tone work. It gets mistaken for a property-dispute warning when it is usually pride in doing the work — the vest signals builder, not menace more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.

conversationExamples.message: announcing a renovation you just started 👷
conversationExamples.interpretation: Family threads are where this lands most naturally. The reading is announcing work, repairs, or a job in progress, and nobody in the thread is reading it as anything sharper than that.
